text:
She saw again that accursed female with goat-like feet, half naked, who, with her right arm raised, seemed to command her to stop. She turned, and on the other side saw Berto, who did not dare move to detain her, did not dare speak for fear of frightening her, and kept watching her, to divine from her gestures the decision she would make.

She returned to her armchair, let herself fall into it, and said not a word.

Thus followed an anguished silence of several minutes, during which Loredana and Berto stared keenly at each other, motionless, as though scrutinizing one another; but Berto could endure it no longer, approached her again, and seized her hands.

“Stay!” he said, his voice veiled by passion. “Stay! I implore thee! I know thou dost not love me, and that does not frighten me....”

He was trying to remove one of her gloves; she noticed, and unbuttoned it with a swift gesture, offering him her bare hand and wrist to kiss; but when she felt those avid lips upon her flesh, she turned her head away as though in revulsion.

“No!” she said. “Wait!”

She seized the goblet and drained it avidly, then held it out to Berto again so that he might pour more, and again she drank; but, catching sight of herself in the mirror, she threw the empty goblet to the floor, where it shattered.

“What do you want to do with me?” she then said.

“Everything thou shalt command me to do,” Berto replied. “I am free; I can leave this very day, tonight, tomorrow, whenever thou askest it of me.”

“Yes,” Loredana declared. “We shall leave at once. We shall go to Rome.”

She burst into such a harsh and sardonic laugh that Berto looked at her in fright.

“To Rome,” Loredana repeated. “I was to go there with Flopi; I shall go with you. Is it not the same? Am I not your mistress? Did they not want me to be your mistress? One man or another, it matters little.... Why do we not go to Sirmione as well?... I want to trample upon all my past, I want to destroy every memory, I want nothing to remain, nothing at all of what was so dear to me and would make me blush!... Ah, you do not know the horror I feel for life!... You think only of taking possession of me; I see it in your eyes, and you do not understand that I am no longer alive, you do not understand that I hate you, and the nearer you come to me, the more I hate you!...”

Berto did not reply, but the hand that held the young woman’s hand loosened its grip; he drew back, struck by the savage vehemence of those words.

“Why do you want me?” Loredana continued, casting him a contemptuous glance. “I love Filippo, and I sacrifice myself for him. Is that not clear? Is it not clear that I want to ruin myself in order to save him? Have I not told you already! And I chose you in particular, so that he may despise me so much that he will no longer seek me!... And you lend yourself to this game?... If I consented to become your mistress, that would be the moment when I loved Filippo most, because it would be the gravest sacrifice I could make for him.... And did you not understand it? How must I tell you that I shall never love you?”

Hemmed in by the ferocious logic, which seemed dictated by that need to bite and destroy with which Loredana felt her whole being vibrate, Berto at first found no answer; then he uttered the one word that explained any madness:

“But I love thee,” he said. “I love thee, Loredana; and I know nothing else....”

The young woman looked at him, feeling that he was not lying; he seemed subdued and vanquished to her, and she pitied him.

“Come,” she murmured, rising, “let me go!”

“Where, where dost thou want to go?” Berto asked, taking a step toward her. “Where dost thou want to go, like this?”

She had made her way toward the door, without a hat, like a madwoman.

Berto looked at her, elegant and slender in her perfectly smooth amethyst-colored dress, gracefully adorned with a strip of dark fur that ran around her breast and along the very hem of her skirt like a little snake.

She was going out, leaving, fleeing; suddenly she had felt that the sacrifice was too repugnant, that it was better to die, to rest, to think of no one anymore, and she had remembered the black, deep canal that flowed before Berto’s house.

The hour was late, the light faint, the people few on that winter evening. Loredana could have thrown herself into the water and drowned there without anyone coming to her aid.

“Where dost thou want to go?” Berto repeated.

They met upon the threshold and stared at one another, he with eyes blazing with desire, she with the lost gaze of despair; but because she wished to go on, he seized her by the arms and held her back.

Loredana again broke into laughter.

In her mouth she had the taste of that mire from which human beings drink, that mire which is all of life, and an unslaked thirst burned in her veins, as though she had swallowed liquid fire....

Someone behind Berto—perhaps the half-naked female with goat-like feet—suggested a thought to him: the young woman would never bring herself either to leave or to remain, either to live or to die; she had to be forced.

He drew her abruptly to his breast, sealed her mouth with his own, giving her so long a kiss that he seemed to wish to drink from her her life, her soul, her blood; he felt Loredana gradually yielding, falling backward, and he followed the movement without taking his mouth from the longed-for mouth, and laid her down upon the broad divan.




XVII.


It was a joyous spring, that of 1894 in Venice. An immense host of foreigners descended from every part of the world, the women and men already intoxicated with delights and desire, their souls vibrating with that sensual romanticism which torpid Venice inspires.

New passions and new dramas sprang up amid that throng of people, and on certain evenings Saint Mark’s Square became a wondrous drawing room through which the fashionable women of New York and Paris, London and Vienna, Berlin and Petersburg wandered, leaving in their wake a trail of exotic perfumes.

They saw Venice through the eyes of legend and history, and their souls were transformed, pouring themselves forth and becoming perverted among the treasures of art and the deathly silence of the voluptuous city. The gondola, slow and caressing, agile and mute, made them dream the erotic dreams and swift tragedies of novels; the night, whether illuminated by moonlight upon the narrow waterways and canals, or dark, or veiled, seemed to them as enigmatic and extravagant as in no other city in the world.
